one_liner: Asymmetric LZ77 codec with near-LZMA ratio whose decoder runs about 3.5x faster than 7-Zip LZMA; compression is slow.
what_it_does: LZHAM is a lossless LZ77-family codec for data compressed once offline and decompressed many times (game assets, downloads). It offers a low-level C API (lzham_compress_init/lzham_decompress_init for streaming, lzham_compress_memory/lzham_decompress_memory for one-shot buffers, reinit() to reuse state) plus a subset of the zlib API (lzham_z_*, or LZHAM_DEFINE_ZLIB_API to remap zlib names). The zlib-style API is source-level only: LZHAM cannot read deflate streams and nothing else reads LZHAM streams. This is the stable v1.x repository with a locked bitstream; the lzham_codec_devel repo adds a stronger parser.
how_it_is_fast: The encoder does LZMA-style near-optimal parsing (greedy at level 0), but the decoder swaps most of LZMA's bitwise range decoding for quasi-adaptive Huffman tables (literals, delta literals, main match symbol, rep and large lengths, distance low bits) that are rebuilt on a slowing schedule set by m_table_update_rate; only the is_match/is_rep style flags use adaptive binary models. Huffman literal decoding is much cheaper than LZMA's per-bit literal coding, and 512 KB blocks found incompressible are stored raw. The decoder is a switch-based coroutine, and the memory-to-memory API forces unbuffered mode, which writes straight into the caller's buffer with no dictionary copy.
when_to_use: Compress-once, decompress-many distribution (game data, patches, downloadable content) where you want an LZMA-class ratio but client decode time or CPU/power matters: lzbench 2.4 shows 273 MB/s decode vs 78.4 MB/s for lzma -6 at the same 64 MB dictionary.
Large solid blocks: README says the decoder only beats LZMA above roughly 1,000-13,000 compressed bytes and wants 10-15 KB+ blocks.
Data with many literals or incompressible stretches, where LZMA's decoder bogs down and LZHAM stores raw blocks.
x86/x64 Linux and Windows, macOS/iOS builds you control end to end (you pick and store the dictionary size and table update rate yourself).
when_not_to_use: When a modern codec fits: in the same lzbench 2.4 table zstd 1.5.7 -18 is 2.7% smaller (25.14% vs 25.83%), compresses 1.3x faster (4.13 vs 3.16 MB/s) and decodes 4.3x faster (1175 vs 273 MB/s); brotli -11 is 7.9% smaller and decodes 1.4x faster (derived from page data).
When compression speed or memory matters: LZHAM -1 compresses at 3.16 MB/s, 4.3x slower than lzma -4, and the README puts compressor memory at about 982 MB for a 64 MB dictionary and 5 GB at 512 MB.
Small blocks or per-record compression: the decoder has a high init cost and the README calls it 'not a good small block compressor'.

When you need the fastest decode at any ratio: it decodes slower than zlib (273 vs 318 MB/s for zlib 1.3.2 -9 in lzbench), and xz 5.8.4's decoder (105-124 MB/s) narrows its lead over LZMA to about 2.2-2.6x.

Inputs above about 2 GB per call, or a need for maintenance: issue #19 reports an assertion and core dump compressing a UINT32_MAX-byte chunk (vector capacity overflow), issue #22 reports lzham_z_compress2 failing on small buffers; 14 issues are open with no maintainer replies.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (CMake on Linux, VS2010 solution on Windows; separate lzhamdecomp and lzhamcomp libraries plus lzhamdll)
integration.dependencies: none (pthreads on POSIX, Win32 API on Windows, for threaded compression)
integration.min_toolchain: C++03; tested by the author with gcc, clang and MSVC 2008/2010/2013; must be compiled with -fno-strict-aliasing on gcc/clang
integration.platforms: x86/x64 Linux, Windows x86/x64, macOS, iOS; FreeBSD/NetBSD and non-x86 Linux (e.g. aarch64) fall back to the ANSI C++ path without unaligned loads, atomics or threaded compression; dictionary 2^15 to 2^26 on 32-bit, up to 2^29 on 64-bit
integration.thread_safety: Separate state objects per stream; the compressor spawns its own helper threads (m_max_helper_threads, -1 = max practical). No other thread-safety statement documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial - the zlib-style API eases porting, but there is no liblzma/xz or 7-Zip LZMA API and the bitstream is LZHAM-only, so it replaces LZMA only where you control both encoder and decoder

gotchas: Dictionary size and m_table_update_rate (and the finer table-interval settings) are not stored in the stream; the decoder must be given the same values the encoder used or it fails, usually with LZHAM_DECOMP_STATUS_FAILED_BAD_CODE.

Harness note: lzbench builds its LZHAM copy (identical to upstream except Windows threading macros) with -O3 -fstrict-aliasing -ffast-math and no -fno-strict-aliasing, although the README says -fno-strict-aliasing is required and the author never tested strict aliasing; the silesia output still passed lzbench's memcmp check, so the numbers stand, but the measured build is one the author calls untested.

Harness note: the lzham -1 vs lzma -4 size win is not like for like: lzbench gives LZHAM a 64 MB dictionary (m_dict_size_log2=26) while 7-Zip LZMA level 4 uses 16 MB in fast hash-chain mode (level 2: 1 MB); at the matching 64 MB dictionary (lzma -6) LZHAM -1 is 10.5% larger but still decodes 3.5x faster. Only levels -0 and -1 were run (lzbench registers 0-4), and the lzbench wrapper ignores lzham_decompress_memory's status code and never sets LZHAM_DECOMP_FLAG_COMPUTE_ADLER32, so the timed decode skips the Adler-32 check (lzbench verifies with memcmp outside the timer; LZMA2 has no checksum there either).

Public-domain dedication (2020-09-15) with no patent grant; v1.x streams are not compatible with the old Google Code alpha streams, and lzbench disables LZHAM on macOS and 32-bit x86 builds because the 64 MB dictionary overflows the address space.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Over Fast LZMA2 or xz only when you specifically need LZMA-class ratio with a decoder that is 2-4x faster than LZMA's and you control both ends (Fast LZMA2 speeds up the encoder, not the decoder). Otherwise zstd at -18 to -22 beats it on ratio, encode speed and decode speed in the same lzbench run, and zstd, LZ4 or zlib-ng are the safer, maintained choices for small blocks.
verified_claims_summary: lzbench 2.4 (gcc 15.2.0 -O3 release binary, one thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, turbo off, silesia.tar) measured lzham 1.0 -d26 -1 at 3.16 MB/s compress, 273 MB/s decompress and 54,740,589 bytes, versus 7-Zip lzma 26.03 -4 at 13.6/73.7 MB/s and 55,936,064 bytes (3.7x faster decode, 2% smaller) and lzma -6 at 3.13/78.4 MB/s and 49,551,059 bytes (3.5x faster decode, 10.5% larger; derived from page data). The README's 3.1x faster archive test on the 10 GB benchmark (7-Zip 9.38 plugin, 64 MB dictionary) is first-party with no hardware or compiler stated.
status_note: Abandoned: code untouched since the 2020-09-15 public-domain relicensing, last commits only edit the README, 14 open issues with no replies; small public-domain C++03 that is practical to vendor for x86/x64 if you pin the format parameters yourself and compile with -fno-strict-aliasing.
